Definition 1. (Knowledge Graph) Given a medical knowledge graph, denoted by $\mathcal{KG} = (\mathcal{E},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{T},\mathcal{D},\mathcal{N})$ where $\mathcal{E} = \{e_1,\dots ,e_N\}$ is the set of entities, $\mathcal{R} = \{r_1,\ldots ,r_P\}$ is the set of relations, and $\mathcal{T} = \{(e_{t_i^{\text{head}}},r_{t_i},e_{t_i^{\text{tail}}})\mid 1\leq i\leq T,e_{t_i^{\text{head}}},e_{t_i^{\text{tail}}}\in \mathcal{E},r_{t_i}\in \mathcal{R}\}$ is the set of head-relation-tail triplets (facts). Additionally, $d_{i}\in \mathcal{D}$ represents the entity description of $e_i$ ,and $\mathcal{N}_v = \{(r,u)\mid (v,r,u)\in \mathcal{T}\}$ stands for the set of neighboring relations and entities of an entity $v$

Definition 2. (Knowledge Graph Retrieval) Knowledge Graph Retrieval (Reinanda et al., 2020) is a module that focuses on efficiently retrieving relevant information from $\mathcal{KG}$ based on the user query $\mathcal{Q}$ . In KGs, information is represented as entities, relations, and attributes, forming a structured network. The goal of retrieval is to find entities or relationships that additionally supply knowledge for LLMs. Particularly, we retrieve knowledge from the matched entities $\{e_j\}$ such as entity names, entity types, descriptions $\{d_j\}$ and even triplets or subgraphs $\mathcal{G}_{e_j} = (e_j, \mathcal{T}_j, d_j)$ .

In this section, we conduct experiments on three datasets to answer the following research questions:

- RQ1 (Section 5.2): Does HyKGE outperform the state-of-the-art Knowledge Graph RAG methods using the same database source?   
- RQ2 (Appendix A.3, Appendix A.4, Appendix A.5): Is the framework we designed effective? What impact does each module have on the overall performance?   
- RQ3 (Section 5.3, Appendix A.3): Does the retrieved knowledge we provide enhance the interpretability of LLMs answers?   
- RQ4 (Appendix A.6): How sensitive is HyKGE to hyper-parameters retrieval hop $k$ and rerank threshold top $K$ ?

Dataset. Our experiments are conducted on two open-source query sets: MMCU-Medical (Zeng, 2023) and CMB-Exam (Wang et al., 2023d) datasets, which are designed for multi-task Q&A and encompass single and multiple-choice questions in the medical field, and one open-domain Q&A dataset CMB-Clin (Wang et al., 2023d) which is the inaugural multi-round question-answering dataset based on real, complex medical diagnosis and treatment records. We use CMeKG (Clinical Medicine Knowledge Graph) (BYAMBASUREN et al., 2020), CPubMed-KG (Large-scale Chinese Open Medical Knowledge Graph) and Disease-KG (Chinese disease Knowledge Graph) as external-knowledge source. Details of datasets are summarized in Appendix A.2. Baselines To fairly verify whether HyKGE can effectively enhance LLMs, we selected the following two types of general-domain large models as the base model and explored the gains brought by HyKGE: GPT 3.5 and Baichuan13B-chat (Yang et al., 2023a). We compare the HyKGE results against eight other models: Base Model (Base) include GPT 3.5 and Baichuan13B-chat, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (KGRAG) (Soman et al., 2023b,a; Sen et al., 2023), Query Expansion (QE) (Azad and Deepak, 2019), CHAIN-OF-NOTE (CoN) (Yu et al., 2023b), Chain-of-Knowledge (CoK) (Li et al., 2023c), Knowledge-Augmented Language Model Verification (KALMV) (Baek et al., 2023), Knowledge Graph Generative Pre-Training (KG-GPT) (Kim et al., 2023) and Summarizing Retrievals (SuRe) (Kim et al., 2024). Detailed description of baselines can be referred in Appendix A.2. Evaluation Metrics. We select EM, PCR to evaluate the multi-task Q&A dataset, and ACJ, PPL, ROUGE-R, BLEU-1, BLEU-4 to evaluate the open-domain Q&A dataset. The detailed descriptions of these metrics are in Appendix A.2.2. Table 1: Analysis Comparison of RAG methods. Average Duration is computed based on GPT 3.5 turbo.

In HyKGE, $k = 3$ , $topK = 10$ , $\delta = 0.7$ , $lc = 10$ , $oc = 4$ . The prompts for LLMs can refer to Table 3. Moreover, for all the baselines and HyKGE, we set the maximum number of returned tokens for LLMs to 500 and the temperature to 0.6. In all baselines and HyKGE, we first use the Jieba library in Python to perform word segmentation, and then use filtered text to filter out tone words and invalid characters following "chinese_word_cut.txt" to avoid errors in knowledge extraction. For a fair comparison, we apply the same W2NER, GTE and FlagEmbedding models for all baselines. Moreover, the parameters of W2NER are optimized with Adam optimizer (Kingma and Ba, 2015) with $L_{2}$ regularization and dropout on high-quality medical dataset (Zhang et al., 2022; Hongying et al., 2020), the learning rate is set to 1e-3, the hidden unit is set to 1024 and weight decay is 1e-4. Similar to previous work (Soman et al., 2023a), because of the randomness of LLMs' outputs, we repeat experiments with different random seeds five times and report the average and standard deviation results. Experimental results are statistically significant with $p < 0.05$ . Implementations are done using the PyTorch 1.9.0 framework (Paszke et al., 2019) in Python 3.9, on an Ubuntu server equipped with 8 A100 GPU and an Intel(R) Xeon(R) CPU.

candidate_windows.section_title: training llms with knowledge from knowledge graphs
candidate_windows.normalized_section_title: training llms with knowledge from knowledge graphs
candidate_windows.window_text:
Indeed, in the medical domain, the performance of the base model significantly impacts the quality of the hypothesis outputs (HO). Our experiments consistently demonstrate that larger models with stronger comprehension abilities produce higher-quality HOs. This finding provides a solid basis to believe that training LLMs on medical knowledge—particularly high-quality medical KGs—could greatly enhance the effectiveness of the pre-retrieval phase.

Incorporating KG knowledge directly into an LLM's parametric memory has the potential to bypass certain challenges encountered during the retrieval stage, such as noise and misalignment when interacting with knowledge graphs. As you suggested, this approach could offer a promising alternative, especially in domains where the growth of high-quality KGs is relatively slow or static.

To explore this idea further, we propose leveraging our high-quality KG to fine-tune or train LLMs, enabling the models to internalize this structured medical knowledge. By doing so, we can potentially enhance the model's ability to generate contextually relevant and accurate outputs based on the internalized knowledge.
